Linert Contact Us Contact Advertise Submit News Statement of Values Terms of Service Public Notices Browse notices Place a notice Latest News Elections board finalizes issues for November ballot By Dan Pompili August 6, 2026 7 min read Trending Mahoning County voters will consider more than a dozen issues in the Nov. 3 general election. Wednesday was the filing deadline for the fall ballot, and a list provided by the Mahoning County Board of Elections shows four additional levies, 12 renewals and eight liquor permit requests. County-wide voters will decide on a 2.4-mill, five-year additional levy for the Board of Developmental Disabilities. That measure would collect $15,522,964 annually and cost $84 a year for the owner of a $100,000 home. MCBDD has not requested new money since 2000, but MCBDD Superintendent Bill Whitacre said the state's demand for local Medicaid waiver reimbursement increased by 38% in 2023. That means Mahoning County's required local match increased from about $9 million to nearly $17 million annually. The budget reduction could leave the board financially insolvent in as little as two years. Whitacre said the cost of providing all MCBDD's services has increased from roughly $60 million annually to nearly $100 million. He said MCBDD deficit-spent $5.8 million last year and is projecting more than a $6 million deficit this year. Without new revenue, the agency could require tax advances from Meacham's office by 2028-29 and eventually be forced to reduce staff and services, though Whitacre said the board could never cut enough to make up for the gap. OTHER ADDITIONAL LEVIES In Boardman, voters will be asked for a 2.75-mill additional levy for safety services. Fiscal Officer Brad Calhoun said last month that Boardman's appropriations will steadily begin to outpace its revenues by nearly in 2027 and by as much as $8.86 million in 2031. Boardman has not obtained additional funding since 2011. The township tried for a 4.5-mill fire department levy in 2024 to generate $6.1 million for EMS services, but that effort failed. In 2025, the township failed to place a 2.5-mill current expenses levy on the ballot for renewal. Funds for that levy, originally passed in 1995, were collected in tax year 2025, but will not be collected in 2026. County Auditor Ralph Meacham said the levy was worth $1.971 million annually. Canfield Schools will ask residents to approve a 5.9-mill, five-year additional levy for operating expenses. Last month, Superintendent Joe Knoll said the district saved $3.5 million from 2020 to 2025 by eliminating 12 employees through attrition and having five accepting retire/rehire deals. But without new money, Knoll said Canfield may have to cut 40 to 50 employees and reduce class sizes. He said the Mahoning County Commissioners passage of an additional 2.5% owner occupied tax credit, which will not be reimbursed by the state, will cost Canfield $380,000 a year. Canfield ended last school year with a $1.25 million spending deficit and Knoll said the district expects a $2.5 million deficit this year. West Branch Schools will ask for a 1-mill, five-year additional levy for permanent improvements. The levy would generate between $440,000 and $441,000 per year and cost homeowners $35 per $100,000. Permanent improvement funds may only be used for projects such as building repairs and cannot be used for day-to-day operating costs or employee salaries. Superintendent Matthew Manley said in June that the district no longer has the 0.5-mill permanent improvement fund included in the bond that was used to build the current facilities 25 years ago. That money was being used to maintain the facilities until West Branch paid off the bond. Manley said the district hopes to use the money for several projects, including energy conservation efforts and roof improvements at Knox Preschool. RENEWALS Austintown Township is asking voters to renew two existing levies: A 0.8-mill, five-year renewal levy for parks that generates $321,610 annually and costs $10 per $100,000, and a 0.5-mill, five-year renewal for the senior center that generates $327,568 a year and costs $11 per $100,000. The City of Canfield will ask for a 3.9-mill, five-year renewal levy for the police department. Originally passed in 2016 and renewed in 2021, the levy generates $812,524 annually and costs $82 per $100,000. Lowellville Schools will ask voters to renew a 4-mill, five-year levy that collects $224,058 annually and costs $107 per $100,000, for general permanent improvements. New Middletown will request a renewal of a 1.5-mill, five-year levy that collects $44,786 a year for roads and bridges, and costs $39 per $100,000. Poland Village hopes to renew a 1-mill, five-year police levy that generates $53,300 annually at a homeowner cost of $23 per $100,000. Springfield Township also will ask voters to approve two 1.5-mill, five-year renewal levies. The levy for current expenses generates $135,515 a year and costs $15 per $100,000. The levy for fire and EMS collects $179,695 annually and costs $22 per $100,000. Boardman Schools is seeking renewal of a five-year fixed-sum levy for current expenses, which generates $4,646,975 annually. District Treasurer A.J. Ginnetti is on vacation this week, but spokesperson Amy Radinovic said there is no millage value assigned to the levy, and it is unclear what the cost per $100,000 would be. Radinovic said the levy, if passed, will not be collected until calendar year 2028. Poland Schools will ask for two renewals -- a 3.57-mill levy, five-year levy for emergency requirements, which generates $2,181,867 annually and costs $125 per $100,000, and a 1-mill, five-year levy for permanent improvements, that collects $403,667 per year and costs $22 per $100,000. LIQUOR OPTIONS In Boardman, Three Brothers Market - Indian Grocery and Sweet Shop, 6607 Market St., is requesting a Monday through Saturday liquor license. Rulli Brothers at 8025 South Ave. is requesting a Sunday permit. The store owners recently decided to be open on Sundays for the first time in its history "to keep up with shoppers' habits." Tobacco City at 112 Boardman-Poland Road is requesting Monday-Saturday and Sunday permits. Millionaire Express at 5955 South Ave. is requesting a Sunday permit. In Youngstown, Gateway Gas Mart at 2732 Glenwood Ave is requesting both a Monday through Saturday permit and a Sunday permit, while Lorenzino's Bocce Club at 128 Jacobs Road is requesting a Sunday permit. In Austintown, Rulli Brothers at 431 Kirk Road also is requesting a Sunday permit. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian View image in fullscreen The ‘Barclays five’ outside Preston crown court on Friday, (l-r) Mohammed Malik, Alma Yaniv, Hmeera Atiqnisar, Amanda Kelly and Brendon O’Hagan. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian Palestine Action Palestine Action ‘Barclays five’ will not be sentenced as terrorists Activists who targeted bank in Burnley were found guilty in June of causing damage exceeding £200,000 Raphael Boyd Fri 21 Aug 2026 10.30 EDT First published on Fri 21 Aug 2026 08.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Five Palestine Action activists who vandalised a Barclays branch in Burnley will not be sentenced as terrorists, a judge has ruled. Dubbed the Barclays five, Brendon O’Hagan, 28; Amanda Kelly, 31; Hmeera Atiqnisar, 31; Mohammed Malik, 28; and Alma Yaniv, 70, were all found guilty in June of causing damage exceeding £200,000, after breaking windows and throwing red paint at a branch of Barclays Bank in Lancashire in August 2024. The group targeted the site in protest at Barclays because it held shares in the Israeli weapons company Elbit Systems. Judge Altham, the recorder of Preston, ruled on Friday that while the damage was substantial, it was not of the size of other attacks or against a sensitive property, such as an arms company, as has happened in previous Palestine Action incidents, and thus did not meet the high threshold for a terrorist sentencing. All five will still be sentenced next month for criminal damage, but will face shorter jail terms as a result of the ruling. View image in fullscreen Supporters outside Preston crown court before the ruling. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian After the five activists were found guilty in June, the trial judge, Philip Parry, told the prosecution and the defence he intended to consider a “terrorist connection” to the offending. It is understood this was a result of new information coming to light during the trial. Neither the five activists nor the jury that found them guilty of criminal charges were aware that the case would be considered as terrorism until after they were found guilty. During the hearings that took place at Preston crown court on Friday, legal representatives for the activists stated that four of them, excluding Yaniv, had admitted to being members of Palestine Action during the trial, but that this was irrelevant, because Palestine Action was not proscribed as a terrorist group until a year after the act of vandalism. View image in fullscreen Police and supporters of the ‘Barclays five’ outside Preston crown court on Friday. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian In a statement put out by the five after the ruling, the group said they were “extremely relieved that the court has seen sense” but said a terrorism sentencing “should never have been an option” and accused the state of “attempting to equate property damage to the Israeli war machine with terrorism”. They said: “A terrorism sentence would not only aggravate our sentence significantly, it would mean we would be imprisoned as terrorists and subject to notification requirements for 15-plus years upon release. Those requirements include notifying police of any new address, bank account, phone number, email address, relationship and more. If we failed to do so, even by accident, we would face an additional five years in prison. “The proscription of Palestine Action, the arrests of over 3,500 people under the Terrorism Act for holding signs and the sentencing of direct action activists as terrorists, are all tools being used by the state to protect the Israeli weapons industry and continue its role in the ongoing genocide in Gaza. “The use of counter-terror powers against direct action for Palestine came after extensive lobbying by the Israeli government, Elbit Systems, pro-Israel lobby groups and politicians with vested interests.” It was reported in October 2024 that Barclays had sold all its Elbit shares. The bank had previously said it held them only in relation to client-driven transactions, being neither an investor nor shareholder in the arms company. Commenting on the ruling, Kerry Moscogiuri, the chief executive of Amnesty International UK, said: “The fact that the defendants in today’s case were not sentenced as terrorists is welcome. No one should be treated more harshly under the law because their crimes were part of a protest against genocide or any other issue, and the misuse of terrorism powers in this way should never have even been considered. “We now need to see the proscription against Palestine Action lifted and an end to the misuse of sweeping counter-terror powers against direct action protesters. The government should begin the process of reversing the years of attacks on our right to protest, one of the most effective tools we have to hold our leaders to account.” Explore more on these topics Palestine Action Crime North of England Burnley Protest news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Supreme court says Palestine Action co-founder can challenge ban on group Palestine Action activists face being sentenced as terrorists over bank damage You may not sympathise with the Elbit four’s methods. A hírt a székesfehérvári Vörösmarty Színház osztotta meg a Facebook-oldalán . „Karcsi hosszú éveken át volt a Vörösmarty Színház társulatának meghatározó tagja. Erőteljes színpadi jelenléte, különleges energiája és emlékezetes alakításai nyomot hagytak mindannyiunkban, akik vele dolgozhattunk” – írta a színház. Kuna Károly tizennyolc évesen, 1975-ben szerepelt a Déry Tibor regényéből készült Felelet című sorozatban. 1980-ban végzett a Színház- és Filmművészeti Főiskolán, pályája során pedig többek között Miskolcon, Kaposváron, Győrben és Székesfehérváron játszott. Stúdió K A Danton-ügy című előadásában nyújtott Robespierre-alakításáért 2010-ben fővárosi elismerést kapott. A székesfehérvári társulat elsőként neki ítélte oda a Vörösmarty-gyűrűt. 2002-ben Jászai Mari-díjat, 2020-ban Aase-díjat kapott. Több tévéfilmben és sorozatban is szerepelt, feltűnt a Szomszédok , a Kisváros és a Jóban Rosszban című sorozatokban is. Hatvankilenc éves korában halt meg. Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem!
